executive_assessment.text: Four named urban study areas provide census-block vulnerability factors; the Juan Lacaze sewer finding is historical, not a statement about current service coverage.
Severe drought affected national agricultural output, while modeled macroeconomic responses and historical relocation evidence have distinct scales and denominators.
Named Paysandú/Salto sites and 2023–2024 flood events document evacuation and service pressures. SATI preparedness is a capacity; neither relocation nor evacuation proves violence.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2020-04-22 reports: Study covers Juan Lacaze, Rivera, Canelones and Arroyo Pantanoso in Montevideo to identify urban risk and priority zones.

Source dated 2020-04-22 reports: 2011 census-block indicators include age under 15 or over 65, severe disability, crowding, insecure tenure, substandard housing, lack of piped water or sanitation, and informal settlements.
Source dated 2020-04-22 reports: Heat vulnerability combines hazard with age, disability, water access and crowding; flood with crowding, sanitation, insecure tenure and informal settlements.
Source dated 2020-04-22 reports: Juan Lacaze had no sewer network in study data; lower coverage counted as higher hydrometeorological exposure.
Source dated 2020-04-22 reports: Local capacity review considers risk maps, risk-informed plans, early warning and government/community coordination.
Source dated 2020-04-22 reports: Maps project hazards to 2044 and 2099; flood and drainage areas remain unchanged without hydrological modeling.

The IMF reports a national agricultural-output decline of 25% year-on-year between late 2022 and mid-2023 during severe drought. Its soil-moisture modeling particularly covers Colonia, Durazno, Flores, Paysandú, Río Negro, San José and Soriano; the national loss is not assigned equally to those departments.

Source dated 2024-01-08 reports: The October 2023–January 2024 Uruguay River flood affected Artigas, Cerro Largo, Paysandú, Salto and Tacuarembó; peak displacement was 3,511 people, over 90% self-evacuated, with the largest counts in Paysandú, Salto and Artigas.

Source dated 2024-01-08 reports: In Paysandú, Diagonal San Félix, the waterfront, Unión Portuaria and the racetrack vicinity were among the hardest-hit areas; in Salto, the waterfront, Arenitas Blancas and Parque Harriague were most affected.

Source dated 2024-01-08 reports: The lower Uruguay River SATI combines meteorological and hydrological forecasts; early warning enabled evacuation before floodwater reached homes, while departmental committees prepared response resources and evacuation centers.

Source dated 2025-01-10 reports: SINAE's 2024 table attributes 13,682 affected people and 5,090 affected homes to 40 floods; flood-row counts include 7,252 women, 6,430 men, 9,065 adults and 4,617 minors. Durazno, San José, Paysandú and Florida had the most people affected overall.

Source dated 2025-01-10 reports: March rainfall totals doubled usual monthly averages; flooding reached Santa Lucía and 25 de Agosto in Canelones and Florida, places described as historically unaffected, and displaced 8,268 people across 13 departments.

known_gaps.text: Automated machine-screening is not independent source verification. Routine/default app-use approval does not certify claims or sources. 15 of 15 evidence records and 0 of 0 pathways lack claim-level verification in this remediation; review the linked records before relying on them.

Reviewed primary reports document climate and hydrometeorological impacts, relocation, livelihood losses and preparedness but do not establish a link to armed conflict, political violence, crime or social unrest.

No primary source was identified in this search showing insecurity or violence obstructing climate adaptation, early warning or disaster response; this is a search gap, not evidence that such effects never occur.

The four-city vulnerability assessment is preliminary, relies on 2011 census indicators and did not quantitatively integrate adaptation capacity; its flood projections lack hydrological recalculation.
The IMF relocation estimate is national and does not identify the affected locations; SINAE provides named event locations but limited demographic, tenure or protection detail at site level.
SINAE's 2024 annual page has an inconsistent hydrometeorological aggregate in prose and its table total; claims use only the flood-specific table row or event-specific reported counts.
No supported climate-to-violence or reverse-FCV pathway was identified. Relocation and disaster evacuation do not by themselves establish FCV.
The four-city assessment uses 2011 census inputs and qualitative capacity review; it is preliminary, and flood/drainage areas were not hydrologically recalculated for future maps.
IMF national economic and relocation findings must not be assigned equally to named study departments. Model shock responses are not calendar forecasts.

The SINAE annual page contains an aggregate inconsistency; only identified event or flood-row figures are retained. Event counts and official response accounts are not independent outcome evaluations.
Routine/default app-use approval granted by Lindsey Jones on 2026-10-27; independent source verification remains incomplete. Lending eligibility is not an FCV classification.
